subject: maths
title: Patterns: what comes next?
intro: A pattern is something that repeats in a way you can predict. Stripes on a shirt, day and night, the tiles on a floor — patterns are everywhere. Spotting patterns and working out what comes next is a big part of thinking like a mathematician, and it is fun.

sections.heading: Repeating patterns
body: A **repeating pattern** is a small part that happens over and over. To find the pattern, look for the part that **repeats** — call it the 'unit'. In a red, blue, red, blue pattern, the unit is 'red, blue', and it just keeps going.
Once you know the repeating unit, you can say **what comes next**. Look at the shapes below: circle, square, circle, square… so the next one must be a circle.

diagram.caption: Circle, square, circle, square… what comes next? A circle!

sections.heading: Growing patterns
body: Some patterns **grow** instead of just repeating. Counting by twos — 2, 4, 6, 8 — is a growing pattern, because each number is 2 more than the one before. To find what comes next, work out the **rule** (here, 'add 2') and use it: after 8 comes 10.
Number patterns like counting by twos, fives, or tens are growing patterns you will use a lot as you learn more maths.

steps: Look at how the numbers change: each one is 2 more than the last.

sections.heading: Patterns are everywhere
body: Once you start looking, you will see patterns all around: the days of the week repeat, a caterpillar's stripes repeat, and a song has a chorus that repeats. Finding the repeating part or the rule lets you predict what happens next.
Making your own patterns with blocks, colours, or claps is a great way to practise — start a pattern and ask a friend what comes next.

practice.q: In the pattern red, blue, red, blue, red… what comes next?
practice.explain: The repeating unit is 'red, blue', so after red comes blue.

practice.q: What is the repeating part of circle, square, circle, square?
practice.explain: The unit that repeats is 'circle, square' — it keeps happening over and over.
The rule is 'add 5', so after 20 comes 25.
It grows by adding 2 each time, so it is a growing pattern.

practice.q: What comes next: triangle, triangle, circle, triangle, triangle, circle, ?
practice.explain: The unit is 'triangle, triangle, circle', so the next one starts the unit again with a triangle.

summary: A repeating pattern has a small unit that happens over and over; find the unit to know what comes next.
A growing pattern changes by a rule, like 'add 2' — use the rule to find the next number.
Patterns are everywhere; making your own is a fun way to practise.
